turns.prompt_text: I currently SSH with IPv4. Is it a good idea to SSH with IPv6, or is it possible?
turns.response_html:
It is both possible and, in many networking environments, increasingly recommended to use IPv6 for SSH. While the underlying security of the SSH protocol remains the same, the networking layer changes significantly.

Is it possible?

Yes. Modern SSH clients (like OpenSSH) and servers have supported IPv6 for over two decades. If your local machine, your ISP, and the remote server all have IPv6 addresses assigned, you can connect just as easily as you do with IPv4.

Is it a good idea?

Switching to or enabling IPv6 for SSH offers several technical advantages, particularly for systems architecture and remote management.

1. Elimination of NAT (Network Address Translation)

In IPv4, you often have to deal with Port Forwarding or complex NAT traversal to reach a machine behind a router. IPv6 provides enough unique addresses for every device to have its own public IP. This simplifies inbound connections to specific hardware without "poking holes" in a router’s NAT table.

2. Future-Proofing and Compatibility

As IPv4 addresses become more expensive and scarce, many ISPs are moving toward IPv6-only or DS-Lite (Dual-Stack Lite) configurations. Being comfortable managing SSH over IPv6 ensures you aren't locked out of newer network infrastructures.

3. Simplified Header Processing

IPv6 headers are designed to be more efficient for routers to process than IPv4 headers. While the performance gain for a single SSH session is negligible, it reduces overhead in high-traffic systems.

Comparison: IPv4 vs. IPv6 for SSH

FeatureIPv4IPv6
Address Space32-bit ($\approx 4.3$ billion)128-bit ($3.4 \times 10^{38}$)
ConnectivityOften requires NAT/Port ForwardingDirect end-to-end connectivity
ConfigurationDHCP or StaticSLAAC or DHCPv6
NotationDot-decimal (192.168.1.1)Hexadecimal (2001:db8::1)
SecurityFirewall-dependentFirewall-dependent (IPsec is built-in but optional)

How to SSH via IPv6

To explicitly force an SSH connection over IPv6, use the -6 flag:

ssh -6 username@2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334

Note on Brackets: If you are using tools like scp or rsync that use colons to separate the host from the path, you must enclose the IPv6 address in square brackets:

scp -6 file.txt [2001:db8::1]:/home/username/

Potential Gotchas

  • Firewall Rules: This is the most common pitfall. Many administrators configure iptables or ufw for IPv4 but forget to update ip6tables. Ensure your server's firewall explicitly allows port 22 (or your custom SSH port) on the IPv6 interface.
  • DNS (AAAA Records): To SSH using a hostname (e.g., ssh server.example.com), you need to ensure the domain has an AAAA record pointing to the IPv6 address.
  • ISP Support: While growing, some residential ISPs still do not provide full IPv6 stacks, or they may provide a "flaky" tunnel that can lead to dropped SSH sessions.

If you have a dual-stack environment (both IPv4 and IPv6 available), it is generally a good idea to enable both. This provides redundancy; if one routing path fails, you can still access your systems via the other.

How is your current server environment set up—are you managing a single remote host or a larger array of machines?

turns.prompt_text: ssh: connect to host arst:arst:arst::arst:arst port 22: Operation timed out I have hid my private information, but the connection did time out, it looks like my mac min, the machine I am trying to connect to, has timed out
turns.response_html:
A "timed out" error specifically means that your SSH client sent the request, but it never received a response (not even a "connection refused"). This usually points to a routing issue or a firewall silently dropping the packets.

Since you are working with a Mac Mini, here is a targeted troubleshooting checklist to get that IPv6 connection established.

1. Verify the Address Type

The most common mistake with IPv6 is attempting to connect to a Link-Local address without specifying the interface.

  • Global Unicast (Starts with 2xxx: or 3xxx:): These are routable. You can SSH directly to them.
  • Link-Local (Starts with fe80:): These only work on the local network segment. If you use one of these, you must append the interface ID (Scope ID) so your Mac knows which network card to send the data out of.
    • Example: ssh -6 username@fe80::abcd:1234:5678:efgh%en0 (where en0 is your local Ethernet/Wi-Fi interface).

2. Check Reachability (ping6)

Before testing SSH, see if the network layer is even alive.

ping6 [your-ipv6-address]

If ping6 also times out, the issue is likely the network routing or a hardware firewall. If ping6 works but SSH fails, the issue is the SSH service or the software firewall.

3. macOS Firewall & pf

MacOS has two layers of firewalls. Check the standard one first:

  • System Settings > Network > Firewall: Ensure it is either Off or that "Remote Login (SSH)" is explicitly allowed.

If that's on, the Mac Mini might be using pf (Packet Filter). You can check if pf is active and what rules it has by running this on the Mac Mini:

sudo pfctl -sr

Look for rules that might be blocking port 22 on IPv6.

4. Ensure sshd is Listening on IPv6

By default, macOS SSH (Remote Login) listens on all addresses, but it's worth verifying. On the Mac Mini, run:

netstat -an | grep "\.22"

You want to see a line showing *.22 or :::22 (the IPv6 wildcard) with a status of LISTEN.

5. Tailscale Interference

Since you use Tailscale for your mesh network, your Mac Mini likely has a Tailscale IPv6 address (starting with fd7a:115c:a1e0::).

  • If you are trying to use the ISP-provided IPv6 address while Tailscale is active, routing conflicts can sometimes occur.
  • Try this: Use the Tailscale IPv6 address instead. It is often more stable because it bypasses local router firewall quirks.

Quick Diagnostic Command

Run this on your local machine to see exactly where the connection is dying:

ssh -6 -vvv username@your-ipv6-address

Look for the line: debug1: connect to address [address] port 22: Operation timed out. If it hangs there without showing a "kex_exchange_identification" message, the packets are being dropped by a firewall (likely the Mac Mini's or your router's).

Are you trying to connect over the local home network, or are you remote?

turns.prompt_text: pinging the ipv4 showing 100% packet loss
turns.response_html:
When you see 100% packet loss on IPv4 alongside a timeout on IPv6, it indicates that the Mac Mini is not just "ignoring" SSH—it is effectively invisible to your current network.

Since you are managing this Mac Mini (likely for your AI agent framework or dev work), here are the four most likely reasons for this total blackout:

1. The "Stealth Mode" Culprit

MacOS has a specific Firewall setting called Stealth Mode. When enabled, the Mac will not respond to ICMP (ping) requests and will stay silent to connection attempts on closed ports. Even if SSH is "on," a misconfigured firewall rule could be dropping all incoming packets before they reach the service.

  • To check (on the Mac Mini): System Settings > Network > Firewall > Options... > Ensure "Enable stealth mode" is Off.

2. Sleep and "Wake for Network Access"

If the Mac Mini has entered a deep sleep, it will stop responding to pings. While macOS has a "Wake for network access" feature, it can be notoriously finicky over Wi-Fi.

  • The Test: If you have physical access, tap a key on the keyboard. If the pings suddenly start returning, your power settings are the issue.
  • The Fix: Go to System Settings > Energy Saver and ensure "Wake for network access" is enabled. If you're using a Mac Mini, you might also want to enable "Prevent automatic sleeping when the display is off."

3. Subnet or Network Isolation

Since you’ve recently moved into a new place in Ames, double-check your router's "Guest Network" or "AP Isolation" settings.

  • If your primary machine and the Mac Mini are on different bands (e.g., one on 2.4GHz and one on 5GHz), some routers treat them as isolated segments.
  • The Test: Use the arp command to see if your machine even sees the Mac Mini's hardware address: 
    arp -a | grep [Mac-Mini-IPv4-Address]
    If it returns (incomplete), your computer cannot even find the Mac Mini on the local physical wire/airwaves.

4. The Tailscale Path (Recommended)

You mentioned using Tailscale in the past. If the Mac Mini is running Tailscale, its "Local" IP might be suppressed or the routing might be prioritizing the Tailnet.

  • Try this: Instead of using the ISP-assigned IPv4 or IPv6 address, use the Tailscale IP (the one starting with 100.x.y.z).
  • Tailscale handles the NAT traversal and firewall punching for you. If you can't ping the 100.x address either, then the Tailscale service on the Mac Mini has likely crashed or the machine is powered off.

Comparison: Is the machine truly "there"?

SymptomProbable Cause
"Operation Timed Out"Packets are being dropped by a Firewall or the machine is Off/Asleep.
"Connection Refused"The machine is ON, but the SSH service (sshd) isn't running.
"Host is down"Routing issue; your machine doesn't know how to reach that IP range.

Next Step: Are you currently on the same Wi-Fi as the Mac Mini, or are you trying to connect from another location (like the Iowa State campus or work)?

If you are remote, the 100% packet loss is expected unless you have a VPN like Tailscale active or a static route set up.

If arp -a returned nothing for that IP, we’ve found the root of the problem: your computer doesn't even know which physical hardware (MAC address) belongs to that IP address.

Essentially, your Mac Mini has gone "off-grid" relative to your current machine. Since there is no entry in the ARP table, the two devices are not communicating at Layer 2 (the Data Link layer), which is why Layer 3 (IP/Ping) and Layer 7 (SSH) are failing.

What this means

  1. The IP is wrong: The Mac Mini might have been assigned a new IP address by your router's DHCP server.
  2. Network Isolation: You might be on the "Guest" Wi-Fi while the Mini is on the main one, or your router is using "Client Isolation," which prevents wireless devices from seeing each other.
  3. Physical Disconnect: The Mini is either powered off, the Ethernet cable is loose, or it's stuck in a "deep sleep" where the Wi-Fi card has powered down.

Step 1: Scan the Network for the Mini

Instead of looking for a specific IP, let’s see what is actually active on your network. You can use nmap (if installed) or a simple broadcast ping to see who answers.

Using Nmap (Fastest):

# Replace 192.168.1.0/24 with your actual local subnet
nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24

Look for "Apple" or "Mac Mini" in the results. If a new IP appears, try SSHing to that.

Using a Broadcast Ping:

ping 192.168.1.255

(Then run arp -a again to see if any new Apple devices populated the list.)

Step 2: The "Mission Control" Physical Check

If you are currently at your desk with your monitor array, check the Mac Mini's status light.

  • Solid White: It’s on and awake.
  • Pulsing/Amber: It’s asleep.
  • Off: Well... it's off.

If it's on but not responding, try toggling the Wi-Fi or unplugging/replugging the Ethernet cable. Sometimes the macOS network stack can hang, especially if it was trying to negotiate an IPv6 prefix that changed.

Step 3: Use Tailscale as the "Backdoor"

If you have Tailscale installed on both machines, this is the perfect time to use it. Tailscale creates a virtual interface that doesn't care about local ARP tables or router isolation.

  1. Open your Tailscale admin console or type tailscale status on your local machine.
  2. Find the Tailscale IP for the Mac Mini.
  3. Try to SSH to that address: 
    ssh username@100.x.y.z

Step 4: Apartment Wi-Fi Check

Since you are in a newer apartment setup in Ames, many managed Wi-Fi providers (like those in student housing or modern complexes) explicitly block device-to-device communication for security. If this is the case, standard SSH and Ping will never work over the local Wi-Fi.

The Workaround: If your router blocks local talk, Tailscale is your only reliable way to SSH between them without buying your own dedicated router to sit behind the apartment's gateway.

Does the Mac Mini show up as "Connected" or "Online" in your Tailscale dashboard right now?

Since the connection is over Tailscale, the "100% packet loss" and "timed out" errors usually mean the Tailscale service on the Mac Mini has either stopped, the machine is asleep, or there is a specific Tailscale ACL (Access Control List) blocking the traffic.

Because Tailscale operates as a virtual overlay, standard tools like arp won't show the device because it doesn't exist on the physical local network in the traditional way.

1. Check Tailscale Status

First, confirm that your local machine can actually see the Mac Mini on the "Tailnet." Run this on your current machine:

tailscale status
  • If the Mac Mini is "offline": The machine is likely powered off or the Tailscale service crashed.
  • If the Mac Mini is "online": Note the IP addresses listed (both the 100.x.y.z and the fd7a:... IPv6 address).

2. The "macOS Sleep" issue

This is the most frequent cause for Mac Minis dropping off Tailscale. Even with "Wake for Network Access" enabled, macOS sometimes enters a "Dark Wake" state where it maintains a heartbeat but refuses new SSH connections.

If you are at the same location, try to physically wake the Mac Mini. If you are remote, you may need a "Wake-on-LAN" packet or a physical reboot. To prevent this in the future, you can use the caffeinate command via a startup script or set:

sudo systemsetup -setcomputersleep Never

3. Use "Tailscale SSH"

Tailscale has a built-in feature that bypasses many of the traditional sshd configuration headaches and firewall issues. If you have it enabled on the Mac Mini, you can connect using:

tailscale ssh username@mac-mini-name

This uses Tailscale's own identity-based authentication rather than traditional SSH keys/passwords, which is often more resilient to local firewall rules on macOS.

4. Verify Tailscale IPv6

Tailscale provides a unique IPv6 address for every device on your Tailnet. If you want to use IPv6 specifically:

  1. Get the Tailscale IPv6 address from the status command: tailscale ip -6.
  2. It should look like fd7a:115c:a1e0::....
  3. Try to ping that specific address: 
    ping6 fd7a:115c:a1e0::[your_suffix]

5. Tailscale ACLs

If you are the admin of your Tailscale network, check the Access Control List (ACL) in the Tailscale admin console. Ensure that there isn't a rule restricting SSH traffic (port 22) between your devices. By default, Tailscale allows all traffic between your own devices, but if you've customized the policy.hujson, it could be blocking the connection.

Comparison: Local vs. Tailscale SSH

MethodTarget IPProtocolBenefit
Local IPv4192.168.x.xStandard SSHFastest, but fails on Guest Wi-Fi/Isolation.
Local IPv6fe80::...Standard SSHBypasses NAT, requires Scope ID (%en0).
Tailscale IPv4100.x.y.zTailscale MeshWorks anywhere in the world; bypasses firewalls.
Tailscale IPv6fd7a:...Tailscale MeshBest for long-term routing stability on mesh nets.

If tailscale status shows the Mac Mini as offline, the issue is physical power or the Tailscale daemon on the Mini itself. If it shows as online but you still can't connect, it is almost certainly a macOS Firewall setting or a Tailscale SSH permission issue.

Does the Mac Mini show as "online" in your status list?
